rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods / Results <U+2013> the authors report their own stakeholder interviews (more than 170 stakeholders in six EU countries) on remote sensing adoption, with qualitative and quantitative data on platforms, crops, applications, remotely sensed area and adoption factors.
rows.notes: The study is an adoption survey of the remote sensing value chain (satellites, UAVs, aircraft) in France, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Slovakia and Spain. It contains no data on soil sensors or precision irrigation systems and no measurement of water use or water savings; irrigation is mentioned only as an application area for remote sensing (irrigation maps in Spain, developing topic in Germany), not as an outcome. No organic systems are considered. The technology in the passage (soil sensors) is not the one studied, and the effect (optimized water use) is not measured.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods / Results <U+2013> the study reports its own interview survey data (over 170 stakeholders, six countries) on remote sensing adoption, remotely sensed area estimates and a SWOT analysis of adoption factors.
rows.notes: The study does not address soil sensors or soil fertility/soil health at all. Its subject is the adoption of remote sensing (satellite, UAV, aircraft imagery) in agriculture; the closest related content is that vegetation-index-based nitrogen prescription maps are a main use, which is remote sensing, not soil sensors, and no soil fertility outcome is measured. Organic systems are not mentioned.

notes: Full conference paper text available (ECPA 2023, pp. 805-812); figures are described but not reproduced. The study is a stakeholder-interview adoption survey of remote sensing in six EU countries and provides no outcome evidence on soil sensors, water conservation or soil health; it appears to be cited in the review for the remote sensing/monitoring clause of the sentence rather than for the soil sensor claims rated here.
